questions.q: A team wants Salesforce opportunities copied into S3 every hour, with no code to write or maintain. Only changed records should move. Which design fits?

options.t: A Glue Spark job that calls the Salesforce API with custom paging code
options.why: Wrong: it works but needs code for auth refresh, paging and retries.

options.t: AWS DMS with CDC from Salesforce
options.why: Wrong: DMS is for databases, not SaaS objects.

options.t: A scheduled AppFlow flow with incremental transfer to S3
options.why: Right: no code, a timestamp cursor moves only new or changed records since the last successful run.

options.t: A full-transfer AppFlow flow on a schedule
options.why: Wrong: full transfer copies a snapshot of all records every run, so it is not changes only.

questions.explain: SaaS to S3 on a schedule with no code: AppFlow incremental.
questions.remember: SaaS source, no code, batch → AppFlow. Only changes → incremental transfer on a timestamp field; full transfer re-copies everything.
variants: The source is an Oracle or PostgreSQL database needing CDC → DMS.
Heavy joins or transforms are needed → land the data in S3, then use Glue, Athena or Redshift.

questions.q: A scheduled incremental AppFlow flow is first activated, but the analysts need two years of Salesforce history. What is the correct approach?

options.t: Run the flow on demand with a date filter first, then edit it to a schedule
options.why: Right: the first incremental run only pulls the last 30 days, so a filtered on-demand run does the backfill.

options.t: Set the incremental offset to 10 hours
options.why: Wrong: the offset is under 10 hours and only catches late-stamped records, not years of history.

options.t: Activate the schedule and wait
options.why: Wrong: the first incremental run pulls only 30 days and later runs only add new changes.

options.t: Switch the trigger to run on event
options.why: Wrong: event triggers react to change events and do not load history.

questions.explain: Backfill with an on-demand filtered run, then schedule.
questions.remember: First incremental run = last 30 days only. For older history run on demand with a date filter, then switch to the schedule.
variants: Records stamped late are missed → add an offset (under 10 hours).
Backfill larger than 100 GB → split into several flows by date range.

questions.q: A company must react within seconds when a Salesforce record changes, and route the change to Lambda or Step Functions. Which AppFlow setup fits best?

options.t: A scheduled flow every minute with incremental transfer
options.why: Wrong: still batch, and many sources have schedule minimums.

options.t: An on-demand flow started by a cron job
options.why: Wrong: manual or API starts are not driven by source changes.

options.t: A full-transfer flow to S3 with an S3 event notification
options.why: Wrong: adds batch delay and re-copies all records.

options.t: An event-triggered flow on Salesforce change events, or sending events to an EventBridge partner event bus
options.why: Right: Salesforce Change Data Capture and platform events can start a flow, and EventBridge rules route to Lambda or Step Functions.

questions.explain: Event trigger or EventBridge partner bus for near-real-time Salesforce changes.
questions.remember: Near-real-time reaction to SaaS change → run-on-event trigger (mainly Salesforce CDC/platform events) or EventBridge partner bus. Schedules are batch.
variants: A routine hourly load is enough → scheduled incremental flow.
Sub-minute streaming of your own events → Kinesis or MSK.

questions.q: A flow writing to an S3 bucket fails with AccessDenied. The bucket is encrypted with a customer managed KMS key. What should be fixed?

options.t: Add an IP allow-list for the AppFlow IP ranges to the bucket policy
options.why: Wrong: AppFlow reaches S3 through a VPC endpoint, so IP allow-listing does not work.

options.t: Add a bucket policy allowing the AppFlow service principal, and give it access to the KMS key
options.why: Right: AppFlow writes with its own service access, so the bucket and key policies must allow `appflow.amazonaws.com`.

options.t: Attach AmazonAppFlowFullAccess to the SaaS admin
options.why: Wrong: that managed policy governs who manages flows, not AppFlow's writes to S3.

options.t: Enable S3 Transfer Acceleration
options.why: Wrong: this is a transfer speed feature and has no effect on authorization.

questions.explain: AppFlow needs bucket policy and KMS key access for its service principal.
questions.remember: AccessDenied writing to S3 → bucket policy for the AppFlow service principal plus KMS key access. IP allow-listing does not work.
variants: Glue table not created → grant AppFlow Glue permissions.
Redshift COPY fails → attach the IAM role to the cluster.

questions.q: Two teams share an account. Each must use only its own Salesforce connection in flows. Which control fits?

options.t: Give each team its own S3 bucket
options.why: Wrong: this controls destinations, not which stored credentials are used.

options.t: Delete the connection after each flow run
options.why: Wrong: deleting a connection removes its metadata permanently and breaks flows.

options.t: Restrict `appflow:UseConnectorProfile` to each team's connection ARN
options.why: Right: that action is the permission to use stored credentials in a flow.

options.t: Store the Salesforce password in the flow name
options.why: Wrong: secrets must not go in names, tags or free text.

questions.remember: Control who may use stored SaaS credentials → `appflow:UseConnectorProfile` per connection ARN (and tags). Credentials live in Secrets Manager, encrypted with KMS.
variants: A SaaS password is rotated → edit the connection so flows keep working.
Who can create or run flows → AmazonAppFlowFullAccess versus ReadOnlyAccess.

questions.q: A flow must pull 300 GB from a SaaS application. What should the data engineer do?

options.t: Split it into several flows using date filters, each under 100 GB
options.why: Right: 100 GB per run is a hard limit.

options.t: Request a quota increase for the run size
options.why: Wrong: the 100 GB per run limit is hard and not adjustable.

options.t: Raise the schedule frequency
options.why: Wrong: frequency does not change the per-run size limit.

options.t: Use the incremental offset
options.why: Wrong: the offset only shifts the time window and is under 10 hours.

questions.explain: 100 GB per run is hard, so split by filters.
questions.remember: Run over 100 GB → split by filters or time ranges, or use another tool. Source caps also apply (Marketo 20 MB, ServiceNow 100,000 records).
variants: A one-time very large transfer → DataSync, Glue or Snow family.
The limits on flows per Region (1,000) are adjustable, unlike run size.

questions.q: Analysts want SaaS data in S3 to be queryable in Athena right after landing, with partition pruning and no crawler. Which AppFlow destination settings help?

options.t: CSV output with no aggregation and no catalog
options.why: Wrong: Athena cannot prune and no table exists.

options.t: JSON output into a single prefix
options.why: Wrong: there is no catalog table and no partitions.

options.t: Mask all fields
options.why: Wrong: masking hides values and does not build tables.

options.t: Parquet format, date partition folders and Glue Data Catalog table creation
options.why: Right: Parquet suits Athena, date partitions allow pruning, and AppFlow creates or updates the Glue table.

questions.explain: Parquet plus date partitions plus Glue catalog.
questions.remember: Athena-ready landing from AppFlow → Parquet, date-partitioned folders and the Glue Data Catalog option (needs a Glue database and an IAM role).
variants: PII in the data → add a masking task, and scan with Macie.
Loading into Redshift → AppFlow uses an intermediate S3 bucket and COPY.

questions.q: Security rules say Salesforce data must not travel over the public internet, and Salesforce supports a private endpoint. What should be used?

options.t: A public flow with TLS 1.2
options.why: Wrong: TLS encrypts the traffic but it still crosses the public internet.

options.t: A private flow using AWS PrivateLink
options.why: Right: traffic stays on the AWS network for supported SaaS apps.

options.t: A NAT gateway for the flow
options.why: Wrong: AppFlow is a managed service and does not run in your NAT path.

options.t: An EventBridge API destination
options.why: Wrong: it pushes events to HTTP endpoints and is not a bulk transfer path.

questions.remember: Traffic must stay off the internet and the SaaS supports it → private flow (PrivateLink). TLS alone is not private.
variants: The SaaS has no PrivateLink option → public flow with TLS and SaaS-side IP allow-listing.
JDBC or RDS PostgreSQL connectors let the database stay non-public.
